blocks.text: Goals of emergency psychiatric care (A-E): (A) Triage — collect first-line information, prioritise by need, escalate appropriately; (B) Assessment — seek diagnostic information, rapidly understand aetiology; (C) Diagnosis — accurate workup for formulation/management; (D) Short-term management — medication, hospitalisation, seclusion/restraint, crisis social interventions, psychoeducation; (E) Discharge planning — preventative strategies and rational follow-up.

blocks.mnemonic: A-E: Triage, Assessment, Diagnosis, short-term Management, Discharge planning
expansion: A — Triage: collect first-line information, prioritise, escalate
B — Assessment: further diagnostic information, understand aetiology
C — Diagnosis: accurate workup for formulation/management
D — Short-term management: medication, hospitalisation, seclusion/restraint, crisis intervention
E — Discharge planning: preventative strategies, rational follow-up

blocks.text: Common emergencies are grouped as general syndromes (suicidality, agitation, confusion, starvation, catatonia, disinhibition) and iatrogenic issues (acute dystonia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, **lithium** toxicity, **clozapine**-related agranulocytosis, intoxication/withdrawal syndromes).

sections.title: 3. Suicide — Epidemiology: National Rate, Sex, Age & Method Patterns

blocks.text: Suicide accounts for 1-==2%== of total global mortality (==1 in 6000==/year) and is the fifth most common cause of years-of-life-lost (**YLL**) in the developed world; it accounts for ==1%== of deaths in England and Wales, totalling 8 per 100,000/year. Rates fluctuate with macro-level socioeconomic conditions (e.g. absolute rates dropped during World Wars); rates are declining in most groups but rising among young men.

National Confidential Enquiry data: global annual suicide rate ==1 in 6000==/year; male:female ratio 2-4:1; most common age is 15-24 for females and 25-34 for males; rates >65 are declining while rates 15-24 are increasing.

Method by sex: men — hanging ~==40%==, drug overdose ~==20%==, car-exhaust self-poisoning ~==10%==, then drowning and jumping. Women — drug overdose ==46%==, hanging ~==27%==, drowning ==7%== (Brock & Griffiths, 2003).

Older people (>75) have the highest national suicide rate; commonest methods are hanging in men and drug overdose in elderly women. Some older adults also die from deliberate self-neglect (e.g. refusing food/treatment). Depression is a strong predictor; social isolation and impaired physical health are other predictors (partly acting via depression); anxious/obsessional personality traits are also important (Conwell 2002; Harwood 2000a/2001b).

Suicide is rare in children but rising among adolescents, mainly males aged 15-19 in England and Wales, chiefly by hanging and car-exhaust poisoning (Hawton 1999a; McClure 2000). Children who die by suicide usually show antisocial behaviour, and suicidal behaviour/depressive disorder are common among their parents and siblings (Shaffer 1974).
There is particular concern in the **UK** about disproportionately higher suicide rates among Asian women.

High-risk occupations: doctors have a higher suicide rate than the general population, with the excess greater in female than male doctors; anaesthetists, GPs and psychiatrists are at particularly higher risk; farmers also have higher rates (Hawton 2000). Possible causes include ready availability of means (poisons, guns) plus work/financial stress (Malmberg 1999).

Suicide is the 14th leading cause of death worldwide (1-==2%== of global mortality); approximately 20 people make a suicide attempt for every completed suicide, though this ratio varies by country depending on the lethality of commonly-used methods (e.g. pesticides in low-income countries are far more lethal than the analgesics/psychotropics typically ingested in high-income countries). Rates of attempts are generally higher in females, but completed suicide is 2-3x more common in males in most countries, likely reflecting male preference for higher-lethality methods and reluctance to seek help.

blocks.text: Suicide rates vary more than 10-fold between countries, partly reflecting variable reliability of suicide statistics (inconsistent coroner recording; cultural/religious acceptability of suicide affecting reporting). Key influences: economic recession (rates rise), changes in access to high-lethality methods, periods of war (rates generally fall), and media reporting of celebrity suicide (transient rises). Suicide is currently the leading cause of death among young/middle-aged men in the **UK**, and death rates among under-25s have been increasing in recent years.

sections.title: 4. Suicide Risk Quantified by Psychiatric & Substance-Use Diagnosis

blocks.text: Frequency of mental disorders from psychological-autopsy studies of completed suicides (Isometsä 2001): depressive disorders 36-==90%==; alcohol dependence/abuse 43-==54%==; drug dependence/abuse 4-==45%==; schizophrenic disorder 3-==10%==; organic mental disorder 2-==7%==; personality disorders 5-==44%==.

About 6-==10%== of people with a mood disorder die by suicide; risk is highest for depressed inpatients and lowest for those treated in primary care. History of impulsive/aggressive behaviour, alcohol/drug abuse or dependence, and cluster B personality disorders raise the risk within major depression; a history of a prior suicide attempt raises risk 40-fold.

Alcohol and drugs (often combined) are a major risk/precipitating factor. Lifetime suicide risk in alcohol dependence is ~==7%== (little variation over the lifespan); the suicide rate in heavy drinkers is 3.5x the general population, and 10x in those with a diagnosable alcohol use disorder. In drug dependence/abuse the risk is ~15x expected.

In anorexia nervosa the suicide risk is about 20-fold higher than the general population. In schizophrenia the lifetime risk is ~==6%== (almost 10x higher than general population); most schizophrenia patients who die by suicide do so in the active phase, after depressive symptoms.

Personality disorders are strongly associated with suicide; most **PD** victims have comorbid depression or substance abuse and often show impulsive/aggressive behaviour. Rates of personality disorder are higher among younger suicide victims.

blocks.text: Bipolar disorder and suicide: most suicide attempts **AND** most completed suicides occur in the depressive phase, not the manic phase. ~==17%== of bipolar I and ~==24%== of bipolar **II** patients attempt suicide during their illness (higher than in unipolar depression); ~==8%== of men and ~==5%== of women with bipolar disorder die by suicide; the standardized mortality ratio for suicide in hospitalised bipolar patients is 15 (men) and 22.4 (women). Bipolar **II** carries a higher suicide risk than bipolar I despite ostensibly 'milder' mood elevation, alongside higher mood-episode frequency, comorbidity and rapid cycling.

blocks.text: In bipolar disorder, most completed suicides (and most attempts) occur in the **DEPRESSED** phase, not the manic phase — a common misconception the exam deliberately targets, alongside the exact attempt-rate figures (==17%== **BP-I**, ==24%== **BP-II**).

About ==35%== of first-episode patients attempt suicide, and completed suicide is most common in the early years of psychotic illness.

blocks.text: Commonest suicide methods overall: hanging and overdose. Most common psychiatric diagnoses in suicide: major depression (30-==31%==) and alcohol dependence (17-==24%==). Mental retardation, dementia and **OCD** carry lower suicide rates than other disorders — **BUT** only if no clinical depression is present.

Of suicides, 40-==60%== had at least one recorded deliberate self-harm (**DSH**) attempt; ==30%== of **DSH** repeats within one year. ==25%== of people who die by suicide were in contact with mental health services within a year of death; ==25%== were on a psychiatric outpatient register.

Alcohol involvement: ==25%== of all attempted suicides occur under alcohol influence, and ==50%== have had alcohol within the previous 6 hours. Of people who die by suicide: ==12.5%== had seen a psychiatrist in the previous week, ==33%== had seen a health worker within 3 weeks, ==66%== had seen their **GP** within 4 weeks, and ==40%== had seen their **GP** within the previous week.

Inpatient suicide: commonest methods are hanging, using a belt or curtain rail. ==25%== of all inpatient suicides occur in the first week of admission; ==80%== occur while the patient is under routine (not constant/intermittent) observation; ==20%== of inpatient suicide victims were non-compliant with medication; about one-third of inpatient suicides involved patients who were on agreed leave at the time of death.

Post-discharge suicide: ==25%== of suicides occur within 3 months of discharge (==40%== of these before the first follow-up); in the first 28 days after discharge, ==1 in 500==-1000 patients die by suicide. Post-discharge suicides are linked to admissions <7 days, a prior discharge within 3 months of the final admission, and higher self-discharge rates. The proportion occurring before the first follow-up appointment is ==40%== in England & Wales, ==35%== in Scotland, and ==66%== in Northern Ireland.

Mental health teams in England regard ==22%== of suicides (especially inpatient suicides) as preventable, and identifiable risk-reducing factors (mainly improved compliance and closer supervision) are noted in ~==67%== of recorded suicides. Nearly ==30%== of community suicides had missed their most recent appointment with services. Enhanced Care Programme Approach (**CPA**) cases account for nearly ==50%== of suicides.

Ethnic minorities: suicide is associated with more severe illness and higher recent-onset treatment non-compliance; ==75%== of Black Caribbean patients who die by suicide in England & Wales have a schizophrenia diagnosis. Homelessness: involved in ==3%== of suicides in England & Wales, ==2%== in Scotland, ==1%== in Northern Ireland; ==71%== of homeless suicides occur during or immediately after inpatient care.

The strongest risk factor for suicide is a history of **DSH** (attempted suicide); risk of suicide within one year of **DSH** is ==0.7%== (~==1 in 100== — ==1.1%== in males, ==0.5%== in females), a 66-fold increase over the general population. Of older patients who died by suicide, ==20%== had visited their primary care physician the same day, ==40%== within a week, and ==70%== within a month.

Roughly ==1%== of patients die by completed suicide within the 24 months following an initial act of self-harm, with risk highest in the weeks immediately following — a mortality rate 50-100x that of the general population.

sections.title: 6. Deliberate Self-Harm — Epidemiology & Comparison with Completed Suicide

blocks.text: Non-fatal deliberate self-harm (parasuicide, attempted suicide) is intentional self-poisoning/injury without a fatal outcome. Across 17 countries (**WMH** survey, Nock et al. 2008), cross-national lifetime prevalence of suicidal ideation, plans and attempts is ==9.2%==, ==3.1%== and ==2.7%== respectively; ==60%== of transitions from ideation to plan/attempt occur within the first year after ideation onset.

Males complete more suicides though females attempt more; ~25 attempts are recorded per recorded suicide. Self-poisoning (mostly prescribed drugs) accounts for ==90%== of **DSH** cases, most commonly non-opiate analgesics (paracetamol, aspirin); antidepressants (both TCAs and SSRIs) are used in ~==25%== of episodes.

Current **UK** **DSH** rate is ~3 per 1000/year; of these, ==20%== repeat within the next year and ==1%== die within the next year; overall, ==10%== eventually complete suicide. ~==33%== of males and ~==25%== of females consumed alcohol in the 6 hours before the act (Hawton 2003b). Deliberate self-injury accounts for ~==10%== of all **DSH** presenting to general hospitals in Britain; the commonest method is laceration, usually of the forearm or wrist.

Psychiatric disorders can be detected in ~==90%== of **DSH** patients seen in hospital settings if standardized assessments are used (Hawton 2001; Suominen 1996); the most frequent diagnosis is depressive disorder, followed by alcohol/drug dependence in men and anxiety disorders in women. Comorbidity with personality disorder is very frequent. Factors associated with risk of repeating **DSH**: age 25-54, alcohol/substance use, personality disorder diagnosis, history of violence, lower social class, previous psychiatric treatment, previous self-harm, single/divorced/separated status, unemployment (Hawton 2000a).

sections.title: 7. Suicide Risk Assessment — Clinical Indicators, Risk Factors & Structured Tools

blocks.text: Clinical indicators of high suicidal intent: act carried out in isolation and timed so intervention is unlikely; precautions taken to avoid discovery or made in anticipation of death (will, insurance, note); premeditated actions (purchasing means, saving tablets); communicating intent beforehand but not alerting helpers after the act; admission of suicidal intent; ongoing plans to repeat and continued access to means; a diagnosable mental illness or personality disorder; physical illness (especially chronic, painful or functionally impairing, e.g. epilepsy, **MS**, malignancy); recent contact with psychiatric services or recent discharge from an inpatient facility.

Risk factors for completing suicide fall into: demographic (older age, male, poor physical health, social isolation, unmarried/separated/widowed, unemployed and living alone); background (past **DSH** especially with high intent, childhood adversity e.g. sexual abuse, family history of suicide or mental illness); psychological/psychosocial (hopelessness, impulsiveness, low self-esteem, recent stressful life event, relationship instability, lack of social support); and current context (suicidal ideation, suicide plans, availability of means).

**SAD** **PERSONS** score: 10 demographic risk factors, one point each, used as a mnemonic risk-assessment tool in acute general hospital settings to guide admission/discharge decisions (see mnemonics and table below).

blocks.title: SAD PERSONS suicide risk score
rows: Male (more females attempt, more males succeed)

blocks.text: Beck Hopelessness Scale: 20 true/false items on pessimism/negativity about the future; scores 0-3 = minimal, 4-8 = mild, 9-14 = moderate, 15-20 = severe risk. Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation: self-report 24-item scale (5 screening items) assessing thoughts, plans and intent; total score 0-48 (each item 0-2); higher scores reflect greater risk, though no defined cut-offs exist for categorising risk.

Risk management plan — four key questions: (a) Is there evidence of mental illness? (b) Is there ongoing suicidal intent? (c) Are there non-mental-health issues that can be addressed? (d) What is the level of social support available? Care of the potentially suicidal patient in the community: full mental health/social context assessment; considering place of safety; regular review of risk and arrangements; safe treatment using adequate doses of preferably less toxic drugs; restricting prescriptions/access to means; involving relatives in safe-keeping of tablets; arranging crisis/urgent access for patient and carers.

Sociodemographic risk factors for completed suicide: male sex, elderly, single/divorced/widowed, living alone with poor social support, unemployed or low socio-economic class — female sex is not one of them, even though females attempt more often. As high as ==90%== of people who die by suicide in high-income countries (e.g. the **UK**) were experiencing a mental illness at the time of death.

sections.title: 9. Managing Agitation, Rapid Tranquilisation & Acute Dystonia

blocks.text: Factors associated with dangerousness/violent crime: younger age, male sex, past history of criminality/violence, childhood physical/sexual abuse or conduct disturbance, psychiatric diagnosis (mania, schizophrenia, alcoholism/substance dependence, conduct disorder, antisocial **PD**, intermittent explosive disorder), a conducive environment, specific symptoms (command hallucinations, agitation, hostile suspiciousness), and unemployment.

Management of the extremely agitated patient: first secure safety of the patient and others, then verbal de-escalation and defusing; pharmacological options are second-line. Drug options and **NICE**-recommended doses/side-effect management are detailed in the tables below.

blocks.text: Acute dystonia is an involuntary, intermittent or sustained muscular contraction causing slow twisting movements or fixed postures, most often caused by antipsychotics (especially typicals); other triggers include antidopaminergic anti-emetics, occasionally serotonergic antidepressants, and withdrawal of anticholinergics used to treat it. Risk factors: male sex, younger age (children/young adults especially), recent alcohol or cocaine use, prior dystonia, dehydration, hypocalcaemia, and high-potency antipsychotics; young female patients are at the **LOWEST** risk. Onset is usually within 1 week of starting/increasing an antipsychotic or of reducing anticholinergic medication.

blocks.text: Two catatonia subtypes present different challenges: withdrawn catatonia requires addressing self-neglect (starvation, dehydration); the agitated/excited variant requires managing dangerousness. Untreated catatonia may cause electrolyte imbalance and renal damage. Beyond depression, mania and schizophrenia, catatonia may accompany neurological conditions (postencephalitic states, parkinsonism, seizures, basal ganglia damage, stroke, tumours) and general medical delirium; **NMS** can also present as catatonia. Most catatonic patients require inpatient care.

**Lorazepam** (1-2mg **IM** or **IV**) is recommended for catatonia, alongside treatment of the underlying psychiatric syndrome. **NMS**, if suspected, should be treated as a medical emergency: the offending neuroleptic must be stopped immediately, supportive treatment instituted (rehydration, antipyretics), and dantrolene (2-3mg/kg) or bromocriptine (2.5-10mg three times daily) considered after transfer to a medical **ITU**.

rows: **NMS**, after stopping offending drug + supportive care

blocks.text: In a patient with catatonia alternating between excited/agitated and stuporous/mute-with-waxy-flexibility states, **lorazepam** is the most likely acutely helpful drug; inpatient care is usually required and **ECT** is also effective. Catatonia subtypes: stuporous/retarded (immobility, mutism, staring, rigidity, withdrawal, food refusal, catalepsy, posturing, grimacing, negativism, waxy flexibility, echolalia/echopraxia, stereotypy, verbigeration, automatic obedience, ambitendence) vs excited/delirious (severe psychomotor agitation risking life-threatening 'malignant'/'lethal' catatonia with hyperthermia, altered consciousness, autonomic dysfunction).

blocks.text: **BAP** guidelines (2020): **NMS** is a medical emergency — stop the offending neuroleptic immediately, give supportive treatment (rehydration, electrolyte correction, external cooling), consider intensive care. Most widely recommended initial intervention is a high-potency benzodiazepine such as **IV** **lorazepam** (1-2mg). For more marked disorder (moderately severe rigidity, temperature up to 40C, pulse up to 120bpm), a dopaminergic agent — bromocriptine or the antimuscarinic amantadine — is recommended to 'release' dopaminergic lock-down. For severe/rapidly progressing disease, the peripheral muscle relaxant dantrolene may be tried; **ECT** is recommended for severe or refractory cases.

blocks.text: In a confused/delirious patient, optimising the environment is the most important immediate intervention: presence of familiar people, a well-lit nursing bay, frequent reorientation, one-to-one nursing, encouraging fluid/food intake, and avoiding polypharmacy (including routine sedatives and anticholinergics that can worsen confusion). Medication can be used if agitated/distressed: **haloperidol** 0.5mg in the elderly (repeat after ≥2 hours if needed), or 2mg oral starting dose in adults. Treating the underlying cause is the definitive long-term solution.

Factors associated with self-neglect in the elderly: advanced age, lack of social contacts, medical morbidity, dementia/depression/alcoholism, poverty and illiteracy, suspicious/mistrustful/paranoid personality, loss of a caregiver, bereavement/other loss events, decreased vision/hearing or other physical impairment. Assessment must include activities of daily living, environmental assessment, cognitive assessment and detailed physical assessment, plus formal, documented capacity assessment for treatment decisions.

In anorexia/starvation, lab investigations should check for metabolic, endocrine, acid-base and electrolyte complications. First-line management is restoring nutrition/hydration (oral or parenteral, depending on medical status). In psychotic depression, severe self-neglect and/or catatonia warrant **ECT**; in anorexia, nasogastric feeding may be required.

bullets.text: Confused/delirious patient: optimise environment first (familiar people, good lighting, frequent reorientation, 1:1 nursing, encourage fluids/food, avoid polypharmacy/anticholinergics); medicate only if agitated/distressed.

Elderly self-neglect risk factors: advanced age, social isolation, medical morbidity, dementia/depression/alcoholism, poverty, paranoid personality, bereavement, sensory impairment; assessment needs **ADLs**, environment, cognition, and formal capacity assessment.

Anorexia/starvation: check metabolic/endocrine/acid-base/electrolytes; restore nutrition/hydration first-line; **ECT** for psychotic depression with severe self-neglect/catatonia, **NG** feeding may be needed in anorexia.

sections.title: 12. Legal Framework — Capacity, Consent & Compulsory Admission (England & Wales)

blocks.text: A patient who has harmed himself but is alert and conscious should be presumed to have capacity to refuse medical advice unless shown otherwise as soon as possible; if appropriate, assessment for compulsory treatment should be arranged. If assessed as incapable (e.g. persistent intoxicating effects of overdose), staff must act in the person's best interests, which may include taking them to hospital and giving immediate life-saving treatment. Capacity may change over time, so consent should be sought before each new procedure where possible. If a competent patient continues to refuse consent and there are no grounds for compulsory treatment, a further attempt should be made to find an acceptable alternative; if that fails, consequences should be explained and discussions recorded fully, the **GP** informed, and the patient allowed to leave with an emergency contact number if they insist.

Section 5(2) applies only to voluntary inpatients (not A&E or outpatients) and must be undertaken by the registered medical practitioner in charge of treatment (the consultant or a nominated deputy, e.g. on-call doctor). While under Section 5(2) the patient cannot be transferred to another ward — they are technically in a 'place of safety' — unless life is at risk with likely irreversible serious harm. Section 5(2) does not itself authorise treatment; that requires common law or the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Section 5(4) allows a nurse of the prescribed class to hold an informal inpatient for up to 6 hours pending medical assessment.

blocks.text: The Mental Capacity Act 2005's five main principles: capacity is assumed unless established otherwise; a person is not unable to decide unless all practical steps to help them have failed; an unwise decision does not itself mean incapacity; actions/decisions for a person lacking capacity must be in their best interests; and regard must be given to whether the purpose can be achieved in a less restrictive way.

Capacity assessment is a two-stage process (decided on balance of probabilities): (1) is there impairment/disturbance of the mind or brain?, and (2) if so, does this make the person unable to make this particular decision? The four abilities assessed: understanding relevant information, retaining it, using/weighing it to make the decision, and communicating the decision (by any means, including sign language or writing). The assessor need only hold a reasonable belief about the person's best interests.

Capacity is a legal, not global, concept: it may be absent for one decision but present for another, and must be assessed specifically in relation to the particular decision required, not presumed absent on the basis of any diagnosis (dementia, learning disability, brain injury, mental disorder, psychosis). All doctors — not only psychiatrists — should be familiar with capacity assessment.

blocks.text: A **CRHT** is a multidisciplinary, community-based team responding rapidly (often same-day) to psychiatric emergencies, typically at the patient's home, aiming to reduce acute admission/bed occupancy. Rationale: interpersonal problems (a major cause of crises) are best treated where they arise; most patients prefer home care (less stigma, less power imbalance); home treatment often costs less; and hospital admission has harmful as well as therapeutic effects.

Key characteristics: multidisciplinary, community-based, rapidly responsive, partnership-working with other **MH** teams, focused on situations where admission would otherwise be indicated, able to facilitate early discharge, lower patient-to-staff ratios (visits up to several times daily, 24-hour availability, response within 1 hour where possible, medication administration up to 4 times daily if required, at least daily progress review), and a gate-keeping role (no admission to an acute unit without **CRHT** assessment first). Patients are usually under **CRHT** care for a short period only, i.e. less than 2 months.

bullets.text: **CRHT**: rapid (often same-day), community/home-based, aims to reduce admission and bed occupancy — home treatment is often preferred, cheaper, and less stigmatising than admission.
**CRHT** is a gate-keeper: no admission to an acute unit without **CRHT** assessment first; response within 1 hour where possible, 24-hour availability.
